To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the stability behaviour of exponentially fitted versions of some classical methods can be much worse than for the original method and that the choice of the space of fitting functions must be carefully selected to assess the quality (stability and accuracy) of the method.

(a) for the classical fourth order Runge-Kutta method (RK4), the stability domain of its EF version is much smaller than the stability domain of RK4; (b) the stability domain of a fourth order EF method is much smaller than for a sixth order EF method; (c) for the classical fifth order Runge-Kutte-Nyström method (RKN5(2,3)), the stability domain of EF-RKN5(2.3) is

1) the size of the region of absolute stability of an EF method is not necessarily greater than that of the underlying classical method, and that 2) the size of this region depends on the choice for the fitting space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stability analysis of the EF methods for first order systems and the choice of the appropriate fitting space.
the numerical stability of exponentially fitted methods for IVPs.
the stability behaviour of EF methods for first order systems and the influence of the choice of the exponential functions used for the fitting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EF methods should not be used blindly.
the EF techniques should be applied with great care.
EF techniques are very useful for improving the accuracy behaviour of the underlying method but the stability domain of EF methods may be smaller than the one of the classical method.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stability behaviour of EF methods must be carefully studied and the results should be used to select the best EF method for the problem at hand.
the stability of the EF methods is not a priori known and it is necessary to compute it in order to assess their quality.
EF methods can be numerically unstable, even when the underlying method is A -stable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to assess EF methods, the stability domain of their underlying classical methods should be computed first and the EF method should be evaluated only in a subset of this stability domain.
the EF methods should be evaluated by their stability behaviour, and not by the underlying method.

the stability analysis of an EF method is a necessary step in order to evaluate the quality of the method and that the choice of the EF space should take into account the stability behaviour of the original method.
